summary.text:
Wiltshire publishes its entire loan book, loan by loan, which almost nobody does. What it shows is a £100m short-term programme built out of eleven inter-authority loans in four months, priced between 4.55% and 5.5% — the London Treasury Liquidity Fund alone lent £30m at 5.5%. The under-12-month maturity bucket went over the council's own 25% limit as a result, reaching 33.66%, and the report says openly why and that the limit will be reviewed.

The driver is named twice: funding the DSG/High Needs Block deficit required more short-dated debt than forecast while the council waited on the government's DSG proposals. Same fact pattern as Worcestershire and Herefordshire — this is now a sector thread rather than three coincidences.

The balance sheet reconciles exactly and paragraph 21 puts a value on the £280.105m of under-borrowing: £5.667m of net benefit, and both steps of their arithmetic check. Paragraph 41 gives five certainty rates for 31 March that match our series to the basis point.

Two market loans remain, both from December 2004 at 4.45%: PBB Deutsche Pfandbriefbank and Dexia Credit Local. Dexia now appears at Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, Oldham and Wiltshire.

officer.subject: £100m from eleven councils in four months — and what it did to your 25% limit
officer.meeting: Overview and Scrutiny Management Committee, 29 July 2026; then Full Council

market.basis: MATURITY profile, CERTAINTY rates (published standard less 0.20)

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the outturn report that went to Cabinet on 25 June, ahead of Overview and Scrutiny on 29 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 79 PWLB loans for Wiltshire at a balance of £397.360m against the £399.360m in your Table 7 — the £2m difference is the loan that matured on 1 June, so we are looking at the same book. Your balance sheet ties too: CFR of £800.068m less gross borrowing of £519.963m gives the £280.105m of under-borrowing you state, and Appendix 1 sums to £499.963m exactly.

Worth saying before anything else: you publish the entire loan portfolio, loan by loan, with start dates, maturity dates, rates and annual interest. Almost no council does that. It makes the report far more useful than most and it is the reason the rest of this email can be specific.

What it shows is the £100m short-term programme — eleven inter-authority loans drawn between December and March, priced from 4.55% to 5.5%. The London Treasury Liquidity Fund at £30m and 5.5%, Croydon, Gloucestershire, Milton Keynes and Newcastle at 5.3%, West Midlands Combined Authority at 4.7%, three lenders at 4.6%, Hampshire's PCC at 4.55%. That is a 95 basis point spread across the same market inside four months, and your Table 8 footnote is candid that it pushed the under-12-month bucket to 33.66% against a 25% limit.

That spread is precisely what we track and what nobody publishes. Every council sees its own trades; none sees the distribution. So whether 5.5% was the clearing rate that week or the expensive end of it is not answerable from inside one treasury, and on £30m the difference between 4.7% and 5.5% is £240,000 a year. We publish the inter-authority picture alongside the PWLB side — July's sector lending was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, which is thin, and thin months are when the spread widens. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

We are not suggesting the strategy was wrong. Paragraphs 8 and 44 explain it plainly — the DSG/High Needs Block deficit required more short-dated debt than forecast while you waited to understand the government's DSG funding proposals — and your paragraph 21 puts a defensible £5.667m of net benefit on the under-borrowed position, with arithmetic that checks on both steps. We would only note that we now hold the same fact pattern at Worcestershire and Herefordshire, both borrowing short against a High Needs deficit and a grant they are waiting on. Three counties doing the same thing for the same reason is a sector position rather than three local judgements, and it is worth knowing that you are not alone in it.

Two smaller things. Your paragraph 41 gives five PWLB certainty rates for 31 March — 5.04%, 5.28%, 5.72%, 6.29% and 6.08% — and all five match our own series to the basis point. You are the fourth council to be five for five with us this summer. Paragraph 42 also states all four margins correctly, including the Local Infrastructure Rate at gilt plus 60 through the National Wealth Fund, which a surprising number of reports get wrong or omit.

And the two market loans that remain, both drawn in December 2004 at 4.45% — PBB Deutsche Pfandbriefbank to 2052 and Dexia Credit Local to 2051. Dexia now appears in our library at Kent, Tameside, Newcastle, Oldham and Wiltshire, and at four of those it has called. Your Table 8 footnote judges a call unlikely because the rates payable are above prevailing market rates, which is the right test — we would only observe that Dexia has been exercising elsewhere, and that Oldham published being offered 6.70% on one of theirs. Worth having in view rather than a reason to act.

On pricing, your PWLB book sits about £53.1m below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve today. Standard caveats and we mean them: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote. Yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

On training, four fit Wiltshire. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets goes straight to the £100m. Liquidity & cashflow forecasting next to it. LOBO loans (legacy) for the two that remain. And Pooled funds (CCLA, multi-asset) for the £17.024m against £20.000m of cost and the override exposure your paragraph 77 flags. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
